SSD failure rates are on par with mechanical drives but the technology in use still can't get around the fact that flash memory can only be read or wrote to a limited number of times before things die, an added issue of flash memory is how the data is actually written. Say you have a file thats 20kb in size and your flash memory is arranged in groups of 32kb seems simply you'll just put your 20kb file into any 32kb cell with 20kb free right? Well the problem there as well as having a limited number of writes you actually have to rewrite the entire contents of that cell all at once, think of it like a scorched earth policy with no bit left untouched. So your SSD's controller says "okay lets find an empty cell, shove our 20kb file in there and be done" you might say the problem is solved but really you've just lost 12kb to well nothing other than the controller trying to be frugal with the reads and writes, you've not lost any performance just a little bit of space is gone. Or is it?

To get around this lost space your controller and OS will try and find cells that it can safely rewrite to minimize waste, your 20kb file now gets a couple buddies to fill up that left over space. Fine, the problem is solved only you've essentially eaten into a portion of your cells limited number of read / write cycles doing this, do too much of it and well your SSD eventually hits a point were it just can't find enough cells in a good enough condition to safely move things around without causing more problems than it fixes. Thats why as SSD's get older their failures become inevitable the longer they are used. None of what I said will help you get your drive working again but for future SSD's you might own its a really good idea to keep upwards of a third of the drive empty just so it can do this movement stuff and has a chance to work around bad cells during the lifetime of the drive.
